newsitem.title: SPAIN: Inflows will stay if Latam reforms - U.S.'s Lipton.
newsitem.headline: Inflows will stay if Latam reforms - U.S.'s Lipton.

text.p: Latin American nations must continue to pursue reforms if they are to retain capital inflows from ever more discerning investors, Assistant U.S. Treasury Secretary David Lipton said on Monday.
Latin America drew large capital inflows in 1996, reflecting renewed economic progress in the region, Lipton said in a speech to the annual general meeting of the Inter-American Development Bank.
But it was not yet clear those funds would stay.

"Markets are learning to judge each country on its own record, rather than as part of an emerging market basket. This means that just as markets have been impressed by recent progress, further progress will receive richer rewards. It also means that slippage will receive swift punishment," he said.

A shock Mexican peso devaluation in December 1994 prompted heavy capital flight that sent Latin American economies into a tailspin. As a result, heavy recent flows have raised eyebrows in financial markets.

In the first three months of 1997, an estimated $14 billion in funds were invested in Latin America after a peak of $51.4 in 1996. That was far more than double the previous peak of $21 billion in 1993.
To secure these funds, the region, which has embarked on a series of reforms to open up markets and foster private enterprise, has yet more work to do, Lipton said.
In many nations, inflation remains in double digits and in some, fiscal deficits absorb too many resources. Growth has been too low.
"The region has not yet completed the first generation of reforms," he said. "But even now attention is turning to a second generation of reforms."
The IADB estimates that regional growth was 3.5 percent in 1996, but said in a report this could more than double in coming years if reforms of labour markets and education are carried out.
"Whether the flood of capital into the region is an opportunity or an omen will depend above all on the recipient countries themselves," he said.
